title: The Guatemalan Doctor Infected Without Consent
event_summary: U.S. Public Health Service physician John Charles Cutler, with Guatemalan government cooperation, deliberately infected over 1,300 Guatemalan prisoners, soldiers, sex workers, and psychiatric patients with syphilis, gonorrhea, and chancroid—without their knowledge or consent—to test whether penicillin could prevent sexually transmitted infections. Researchers used prostitutes carrying the diseases, direct inoculation into spinal punctures, and abrasions on genitals to ensure infection. At least 83 subjects died, and hundreds more suffered lifelong damage, with many never receiving adequate treatment.
why_forgotten: The experiments were deliberately concealed by U.S. officials for over sixty years; the records were buried in archives until historian Susan Reverby accidentally uncovered them in 2010 while researching the Tuskegee syphilis study. Guatemala's political instability and the power imbalance between the two nations ensured no accountability, and Cold War priorities kept U.S. medical misconduct from scrutiny.
why_it_matters: The revelation forced a formal apology from President Obama in 2010 and triggered a presidential bioethics commission review that reshaped modern international research ethics guidelines. It exposed how the Tuskegee scandal was not an isolated incident but part of a broader pattern of exploiting vulnerable populations in the Global South—a legacy that fuels vaccine hesitancy and medical distrust in Latin America and developing nations to this day.
